subject: How to include species that have arisen elsewhere

messages.author: 261e2deffe04f642
messages.subject: How to include species that have arisen elsewhere
parts:
Hi all,

I've got a phylogeny of all the species in a family that occur on an island and I want to look at transition rates between three different areas. In addition to endemic and native species, the phylogeny includes the exotic species which are now found on this island. Effectively this means there are gaps in the phylogeny because of all the exotic species in that family that aren't on the island. So if I went ahead and ran BioGeoBEARS on it as is, the rates of shift between areas would not be representative of reality.

I was wondering if one way around it would be to have a 4th state of outside the island to use for all the exotic species. Maybe even multiple ones representing broad geographic areas outside. That would make shifts from elsewhere in the world onto the island separate to the within island shifts.  Do you think that would that make sense?

As a back-up I was planning to run a separate analysis for each monophyletic endemic clade, as we know each of those species originated on the island.  But it would mean a series of quite small clades because of the nature of that family.

I'm interested to hear any thoughts on this.

Thanks,

Esther

> island and I want to look at transition rates between three different
> areas. In addition to endemic and native species, the phylogeny includes
> the exotic species which are now found on this island. Effectively this
> means there are gaps in the phylogeny because of all the exotic species in
> that family that aren't on the island. So if I went ahead and ran
> BioGeoBEARS on it as is, the rates of shift between areas would not be
> representative of reality.
>
> I was wondering if one way around it would be to have a 4th state of
> outside the island to use for all the exotic species. Maybe even multiple
> ones representing broad geographic areas outside. That would make shifts
> from elsewhere in the world onto the island separate to the within island
> shifts.  Do you think that would that make sense?
>

My take is that adding a fourth area representing "outside" is basically
fine, as a model, recognizing as always that "all models are wrong, some
are useful" (George Box), etc.

This is particularly the case if the study region/islands are quite
isolated (e.g. Hawaii) and so "everywhere else" is a reasonably discrete
category.

Of course, this strategy would mean that you would lose whatever might be
interesting about having multiple outside source areas, but this might be
justified in terms of computational run time or just simplicity to focus on
the study question.


Two other thoughts:

- If the goal is to include exotic species that were introduced with
humans, then you have to think quite carefully about how BioGeoBEARS should
be used in that situation.  Typically, BioGeoBEARS is used on phylogenies
that span millions of years, and typically human-introduced exotics came in
in just the last few hundred/thousand years (e.g. 0.001 million years or
less).

Therefore, naively including exotic species in a BioGeoBEARS analysis will
have drastic effects, because without constraints, the analysis will assume
that most of those dispersal events happened over the last few million
years, rather than very recently.

A non-naive analysis might be something like this:

(each of these topics/keywords should be googled, if you haven't heard of
them)


1. Do a time-stratified analysis

2. Set up a very very recent time-bin for the "humans showed up" time bin
(the Anthropocene, perhaps)

2.5. (This may require double-checking that you haven't created any
branches so short they get treated as direct ancestors)

3. Just below the time-bin, use the fixnode and fixlikes options to
*exclude* exotic species from the study region before they arrived there
anthropogenically. This will force all anthropogenic dispersal events to
happen in the Anthropocene

4. Clearly this implies different dispersal rates pre- and post-human
arrival, so along with time-stratification, include a manual dispersal
multiplier matrix, with e.g. a 0.001 multiplier for the pre-human time-bin,
and 1 for the post-human time bin.

4.5 Turn on the exponent (parameter w I think) so that the pre-human
time-bin dispersal rates are now d_base_rate *
manual_dispersal_multiplier^w.  Estimating w will then give you a
measurement of how much different the dispersal rate was pre-human (it will
be 0.001^w times lower).

I just came up with this, so there might be holes, but that's the rough
idea.

As a back-up I was planning to run a separate analysis for each
> monophyletic endemic clade, as we know each of those species originated on
> the island.  But it would mean a series of quite small clades because of
> the nature of that family.
>
> I'm interested to hear any thoughts on this.
>

Having one big phylogeny would be better, as long as you have reasonably
decent sampling of species both outside and inside your study region.
Obviously, weird biogeographical inference would happen if you included all
of the species from the study region, but left out most/all of the species
living elsewhere.

Depending on feasibility, you could use an intermediate strategy also,
with several smaller clades -- but running multiple clades at once under
the same commonly inferred biogeography model would take a bit of new
coding, I won't have time in the near future but I'm sure someone could
figure it out.

Cheers!
Nick


PS - Re: this:
" I was wondering if one way around it would be to have a 4th state of outside the island to use for all the exotic species."

Clarification: areas != states

States are made up of some number of areas

DNA state space: A,C,G,T (4 states)
Binary character state space: 0, 1 (2 states)

But with biogeography:

E.g. areas: A, B
States in the state space: null, A, B, AB (4 states)

Cheers,
Nick



>
> Thanks,
>
> Esther

messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Re: How to include species that have arisen elsewhere
parts:
Hi -- the main risk I was thinking of was something like this:

sp1 - A
sp2 - B
sp3 - A
sp4 - B
sp5 - A
sp6 - B
sp7 - B
sp8 - B
sp9 - B
sp10 - B

Imagine these species have a comb tree with sp10 as the deepest branch.

If you just used sp1, sp3, and sp5 in your analysis, you would estimate region A as the ancestral range, but this would be catastrophically wrong.

You can imagine the weirdness if you had, say, a phylogeny of Hawaiian birds, but only did your analysis on the phylogeny of the Hawaiian birds, leaving out all of their relatives elsewhere.  You would incorrectly infer that the common ancestor of the Hawaiian goose and the Hawaiian honeycreeper lived in Hawaii.

This could possibly be fixed in various ways -- fixnode constraints to exclude Hawaiian ancestors etc., but it would be easier probably to include sufficient outgroups that the source area for each clade can be determined.

Cheers!

messages.subject: Re: How to include species that have arisen elsewhere
parts:
Hi again Nick,

to follow along with your Hawaiian analogy, imagine you were looking at transitions between habit types A and B of Hawaiian honeycreepers within Hawaii. Would including a few species outside the clade from elsewhere in the world as a different habitat type (lets say C), impact on estimates of transitions between A and B for the Hawaiian honeycreepers? 

Would it differ if scaled up to multiple Hawaiian clades of interest (occurring in habitats A and B) with a variety of non-Hawaiian species (habitat C) in between the clades?

Thanks heaps,

Esther
